items.section_title: 1.4 · Objectives 1–3 — Allergy and the red eye
items.html: Rebound hyperemia from ocular vasoconstrictors. Alpha-adrenergic agonist drops constrict vessels to reduce redness and conjunctival edema; constant activation downregulates alpha-1 receptors, so on stopping, vessels dilate because fewer receptors remain for endogenous noradrenaline and adrenaline.

src.question: A patient has used an over-the-counter redness-relieving eye drop daily for a month. On stopping it, the eye becomes redder than before. What has happened?
src.key: Rebound hyperemia, from downregulation of alpha-1 receptors
src.explanation: These are alpha-adrenergic agonists that vasoconstrict to reduce redness and conjunctival edema. Constant activation downregulates the receptors, so when the drug stops there are fewer left for endogenous noradrenaline and adrenaline to act on, and the vessels dilate.

items.section_title: 1.4 · Objectives 1–3 — Allergy and the red eye
items.html: Over-the-counter ocular vasoconstrictors. Use them for under two weeks because of rebound hyperemia, and see a provider if no better in 72 hours, since a red eye that is not improving may be more serious than allergy.

src.question: How long may an over-the-counter ocular vasoconstrictor be used, and what should the patient be told if there is no improvement?
src.key: Under two weeks; see a provider if no better in 72 hours
src.explanation: Short-term use only, because of rebound hyperemia. And the 72-hour rule exists because a red eye that is not improving may be something more serious than allergy.

items.section_title: 1.4 · Objectives 1–3 — Allergy and the red eye
items.html: Vasoconstrictor allergy drops. The vasoconstrictor activates alpha-adrenergic receptors on vessels, reducing conjunctival edema and redness. It treats the appearance rather than the allergy, so it is paired with an antihistamine in products such as Naphcon-A.

src.question: How does the vasoconstrictor component of an over-the-counter allergy drop reduce redness?
src.key: It activates alpha-adrenergic receptors on vessels
src.explanation: Constricting those vessels reduces conjunctival edema and the visible redness. It treats the appearance rather than the allergy, which is why it is paired with an antihistamine in products such as Naphcon-A.

items.section_title: 1.4 · Objectives 1–3 — Allergy and the red eye
items.html: Over-the-counter ocular antihistamine. Ketotifen is an ocular antihistamine available over the counter.

src.question: Which of these is an ocular antihistamine available over the counter?
src.explanation: It is the one marked over the counter in the antihistamine list, which matters because it is what a patient may already have tried before they reach you.

items.html: Cyclosporine drops counseling. Warn patients about ocular burning, which occurs in roughly seventeen percent (about one in six), along with foreign body sensation and blurred vision; warning up front helps keep patients on a drug that takes time to work.

src.question: What should a patient starting cyclosporine drops be warned about?
src.key: Ocular burning, which affects about one in six
src.explanation: Burning occurs in roughly seventeen percent, along with foreign body sensation and blurred vision. Warning about it up front is what keeps a patient on a drug that takes time to work.

items.section_title: 1.1 · Objective 4 — Getting a drug into the eye, and out again
items.html: Prodrugs in the eye. The eye metabolizes some drugs, which is exploited deliberately: dipivefrin becomes epinephrine and latanoprost becomes prostaglandin F2-alpha once inside.

src.question: Latanoprost and dipivefrin are both given in an inactive form. What does the eye do with them?
src.key: It metabolizes them — they are prodrugs activated in the eye
src.explanation: Some drugs are metabolized within the eye itself, which is exploited deliberately: dipivefrin becomes epinephrine and latanoprost becomes prostaglandin F2-alpha once inside.

items.html: Changing spectrum of ocular infection. The spectrum is not fixed; for example, Haemophilus influenzae fell after vaccination was introduced, which changes what empiric therapy has to cover.

src.question: Why has the microbiological spectrum of ocular infection shifted over time, by the example given?
src.explanation: The spectrum is not fixed — the example given is the fall in Haemophilus influenzae after the vaccine was introduced, which changes what empiric therapy has to cover.

items.html: Bacterial conjunctivitis in contact lens wearers. With keratitis ruled out, a fluoroquinolone is preferred for Pseudomonas cover, since contact lens use raises the risk of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a gram-negative rod. Fluoroquinolones are also preferred for corneal ulcers for the same reason.

src.question: A contact lens wearer has bacterial conjunctivitis and keratitis has been ruled out. Which class is preferred, and why?
src.explanation: Contact lens use raises the risk of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a gram-negative rod, and the fluoroquinolones are the class that covers it. They are also the preferred choice for corneal ulcers for the same reason.

items.html: Adenoviral conjunctivitis. No antiviral is indicated; it runs its own course and irritation is relieved. The ocular antivirals exist for keratitis, herpes zoster ophthalmicus and retinitis.

src.question: A patient has adenoviral conjunctivitis. Which antiviral is indicated?
src.explanation: There is no antiviral for viral conjunctivitis caused by adenoviruses. It runs its own course and you relieve the irritation. The ocular antivirals exist for keratitis, herpes zoster ophthalmicus and retinitis.

items.html: Risk factors for ophthalmic fungal infection. These are trauma, chronic ocular surface disease, contact lens wear and immunosuppression; topical corticosteroid use counts as immunosuppression and is the one a clinician can introduce by prescribing.

src.question: Which risk factor for ophthalmic fungal infection is one a clinician can create?
src.explanation: The risk list is trauma, chronic ocular surface disease, contact lens wear and immunosuppression — and topical steroid use is named explicitly as immunosuppression. It is the only one on the list you can introduce by prescribing.

items.html: Trifluridine adverse effect. Beyond ocular irritation, trifluridine specifically causes punctate keratopathy.

src.question: Beyond ocular irritation, which adverse effect is specific to trifluridine?
src.explanation: It is worth separating from the generic irritation every ophthalmic drug can cause, because this one names a drug and an actual corneal finding.

items.html: Aspirin and cyclooxygenase. Aspirin inhibits cyclooxygenase irreversibly and non-competitively. A platelet has no nucleus and cannot make fresh enzyme, so one exposure disables it for its lifetime.

src.question: How does aspirin act on cyclooxygenase, and what follows from it?
src.key: Irreversibly and non-competitively, so the platelet never recovers
src.explanation: A platelet has no nucleus and cannot make fresh enzyme, so one exposure disables it for its lifetime. Everything distinctive about aspirin as an antiplatelet follows from that.

items.html: Ibuprofen with lithium. Ibuprofen reduces lithium excretion, so levels rise; lithium has little margin between useful and toxic, so anything that slows its removal matters quickly.

src.question: A patient on lithium is started on ibuprofen. What is the concern?
src.key: Ibuprofen reduces lithium excretion, so levels rise
src.explanation: Lithium has little margin between useful and toxic, so anything that slows its removal matters quickly.

items.html: Ibuprofen with a diuretic and an ACE inhibitor. Renal function should be watched: the kidney is at risk with the diuretic, and the ACE inhibitor works less well, so its blood pressure response should also be watched.

src.question: A patient on a diuretic and an ACE inhibitor starts taking ibuprofen regularly. What should be watched?
src.explanation: Two interactions at once: the kidney is at risk with the diuretic, and the ACE inhibitor works less well. The blood pressure response to the ACE inhibitor.

items.html: Reye's syndrome. It affects children, with mortality around half; the severity justifies a blanket restriction on a cheap and otherwise useful drug.

src.question: Who is affected by Reye's syndrome, and how dangerous is it?
src.explanation: The severity is what justifies a blanket restriction on a cheap and otherwise useful drug.

items.html: Ibuprofen and age. Ibuprofen is avoided in young infants, as there is a lower age limit below which it is not used, which distinguishes it from acetaminophen.

src.question: Ibuprofen is avoided below a certain age. Which group?
src.explanation: There is a lower age limit below which it is not used, which distinguishes it from acetaminophen.

items.section_title: 2.10 · Objectives 9–10 — Protocols, monitoring and patient education
items.html: Aspirin for fever: other medicines. Patients should not take other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs alongside it; they share a mechanism, so combining them adds the harms without adding the benefit.

src.question: A patient is started on aspirin for fever. What should they be told about other medicines?
src.key: Do not take other anti-inflammatory drugs alongside it
src.explanation: They share a mechanism, so combining them adds the harms without adding the benefit. That means the non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs specifically.

items.html: Tinnitus with regular aspirin. Ringing in the ears is an audible marker that exposure has climbed from analgesia into the anti-inflammatory range.

src.question: A patient taking aspirin regularly develops ringing in the ears. What does that suggest?
src.key: Exposure has reached the anti-inflammatory range
src.explanation: Tinnitus is the audible marker that the patient has climbed the ladder from analgesia into the anti-inflammatory range, which makes it useful rather than incidental.

items.html: Who should avoid ibuprofen. Avoid it in patients with asthma it may worsen, previous ulcer or perforation, or renal impairment; asthma is the easiest to forget.

src.question: Which patients should avoid ibuprofen?
src.key: Those with asthma it may worsen
src.explanation: Asthma is the one most easily forgotten, because it is not an obvious consequence of blocking prostaglandin synthesis. Previous ulcer or perforation, or renal impairment.

items.section_title: 2.10 · Objectives 9–10 — Protocols, monitoring and patient education
items.html: Aspirin for fever: when to return. Patients are told to come back straight away if the fever does not come down, meaning it fails to respond to the medicine rather than merely persisting.

src.question: A patient takes aspirin for fever. When are they told to come back straight away?
src.key: If the fever does not come down
src.explanation: The instruction is about the fever failing to respond, which is a different signal from the fever simply continuing. That is, if it fails to respond to the medicine rather than merely persisting.

items.html: Settings for oral candidiasis. Oral candidiasis occurs with inhaled steroids, HIV infection and chemotherapy, which share suppressed local or general immunity.

src.question: A patient using an inhaled steroid develops oral candidiasis. Which of these situations is NOT given as a setting for it?
src.explanation: Correct -- this is not one of them. The settings given are inhaled steroids, HIV infection and chemotherapy, all of which share suppressed local or general immunity.

items.html: Nystatin. As a nonabsorbable antifungal it acts only where it touches and not elsewhere, which makes it well tolerated but unable to treat anything beyond the mucosa.

src.question: Nystatin is classified as a nonabsorbable antifungal. Why does that matter?
src.key: It acts only where it touches, and not elsewhere
src.explanation: Being nonabsorbable is both the safety of the drug and its limitation: it is why it is well tolerated and why it cannot treat anything beyond the mucosa.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Objectives 1–6 — Histamine and the H1 antagonists
items.html: Histamine H2 receptors in the heart. Through H2 receptors, histamine increases cardiac contractility.

src.question: What effect does histamine have on the heart through H2 receptors?
src.explanation: A cardiac action is easy to miss in a receptor filed under the stomach.

items.section_title: 2.10 · Objectives 9–10 — Protocols, monitoring and patient education
items.html: Nasal spray technique. Do not tilt the head back, because that draws the medicine into the throat, wasting the dose and producing the bitter taste that stops people using the spray.

src.question: Why is a patient told not to tilt the head back when using a nasal spray?
src.key: It draws the medicine into the throat
src.explanation: It wastes the dose and produces the bitter taste, which is the complaint that stops people using the spray at all.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Objectives 1–6 — Histamine and the H1 antagonists
items.html: Indications for H1 antagonists. These are allergic reactions, motion sickness and vestibular symptoms, sleep remedies, and an adjuvant role in anaphylaxis; bacterial sinusitis is not among them.

src.question: Which of these is NOT among the listed indications for H1 antagonists?
src.explanation: Correct -- this is not one. The indications are allergic reactions, motion sickness and vestibular symptoms, sleep remedies, and an adjuvant role in anaphylaxis.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Objectives 1–6 — Histamine and the H1 antagonists
items.html: H1 receptor signaling. H1 receptors raise intracellular calcium through phospholipase C, producing IP3 and DAG, whereas H2 receptors work through adenylate cyclase and cyclic AMP.

src.question: Through which second messenger pathway do H1 receptors raise intracellular calcium?
src.key: Phospholipase C, producing IP3 and DAG
src.explanation: It is the contrast with H2 that matters: H1 works through phospholipase C, H2 through adenylate cyclase and cyclic AMP.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Objectives 1–6 — Histamine and the H1 antagonists
items.html: First generation antihistamines. Beyond histamine receptors they act on muscarinic and serotonergic systems, which gives uses and side effects unrelated to allergy, including antiemetic action.

src.question: Beyond histamine receptors, what else do first generation agents act on?
src.explanation: Acting on several receptor families is what gives them uses and side effects that have nothing to do with allergy. With antiemetic action.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Objectives 1–6 — Histamine and the H1 antagonists
items.html: Paradoxical excitation. First generation antihistamines can cause excitation rather than sleepiness at higher exposure, particularly in children, so an agitated child may have had more of the drug rather than less.

src.question: A child given a first generation antihistamine becomes restless and agitated rather than sleepy. How is that explained?
src.key: Excitation occurs at higher exposure, and particularly in children
src.explanation: The paradox is recognized rather than unusual, and it means an agitated child may have had more of the drug rather than less.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Objectives 1–6 — Histamine and the H1 antagonists
items.html: Azelastine nasal spray. Side effects are a bitter taste and nosebleed; the bitter taste comes from spray running back into the throat and is a common reason patients stop it.

src.question: What side effects are described for azelastine nasal spray?
src.explanation: The bitter taste is the common reason patients stop it, and it comes from spray running back into the throat.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Objectives 1–6 — Histamine and the H1 antagonists
items.html: H1 versus H2 vasodilation. Both cause vasodilation, but H1 is rapid in onset and short-lived while H2 is slow in onset and long-lasting, so blocking H1 alone does not abolish the flush.

src.question: H1 and H2 receptors both cause vasodilation. How do the two differ?
src.key: H1 is rapid in onset and short-lived
src.explanation: Same end result by two different routes and on two different timescales, which is why blocking H1 alone does not abolish the flush. H2 is slow in onset and long-lasting.

items.html: Prednisone in diabetes. Glucose control will worsen: the steroid raises glucose and blunts the drugs used to lower it, so antidiabetic medicines work less well.

src.question: A patient with diabetes is started on a course of prednisone. What should be anticipated?
src.explanation: Two effects pointing the same way: the steroid raises glucose and blunts the drugs used to lower it. Antidiabetic medicines will work less well.

items.html: Stopping corticosteroids. After more than about a week of use, do not stop abruptly, because stopping suddenly produces rebound symptoms; a short course and a long one are stopped differently.

src.question: Why is a patient who has taken a corticosteroid for more than about a week told not to stop abruptly?
src.explanation: It is the duration that creates the problem, which is why a short course and a long one are stopped differently.

items.html: Pseudoephedrine versus oxymetazoline. Pseudoephedrine has the same alpha agonist mechanism as oxymetazoline but is taken orally.

src.question: How does pseudoephedrine differ from oxymetazoline in mechanism and route?
src.key: Same alpha agonist mechanism, but taken orally
src.explanation: The mechanism is shared; taking it orally is what changes both its usefulness and its side effect profile.

items.html: Oxymetazoline systemic effect. Besides rebound congestion, oxymetazoline can raise blood pressure, since a drug sprayed into the nose still reaches the circulation.

src.question: Besides rebound congestion, what systemic effect is described with oxymetazoline?
src.explanation: A drug sprayed into the nose still reaches the circulation, which is what makes it worth asking about in a hypertensive patient.

items.html: Pseudoephedrine and antihypertensives. Pseudoephedrine reduces the effect of antihypertensive medicines, so a patient can undo blood pressure treatment with an over-the-counter product.

src.question: A patient treated for hypertension asks about pseudoephedrine for a cold. What is the concern?
src.key: It reduces the effect of antihypertensive medicines
src.explanation: A patient can undo their blood pressure treatment with something bought off the shelf, without ever mentioning it as a medicine.

items.html: Pseudoephedrine adverse effects. These are fast heart rate, raised blood pressure and headache, all following from stimulating alpha receptors throughout the body rather than only in the nose.

src.question: What adverse effects are described with pseudoephedrine?
src.explanation: All three follow from stimulating alpha receptors throughout the body rather than only in the nose. Raised blood pressure and headache.

items.section_title: 2.9 · Objectives 1–7 — Cough: antitussives, expectorants and mucolytics
items.html: Benzonatate capsules. Swallow them whole, because they release local anesthetic that numbs whatever it touches; releasing it in the mouth and throat numbs the airway the patient needs to protect.

src.question: Why must a benzonatate capsule be swallowed whole?
src.key: It releases local anesthetic into the mouth
src.explanation: It numbs whatever it touches, so releasing it in the mouth numbs the airway a patient needs to protect. And into the throat, which is the airway the patient needs to protect.

items.html: Clonidine with a beta blocker. Together they lower pressure, but abrupt clonidine withdrawal in this combination produces a dramatic rise in blood pressure.

src.question: A patient takes clonidine together with a beta blocker. What happens to blood pressure if the clonidine is stopped abruptly?
src.explanation: While both are taken they lower pressure together, but abrupt clonidine withdrawal in this combination produces a dramatic rise in blood pressure.

items.html: Hydralazine contraindications. It is contraindicated in coronary artery disease, the elderly and ischemia, because vasodilation with reflex sympathetic activation raises cardiac workload.

src.question: In which patient is hydralazine contraindicated?
src.key: An older adult with coronary disease
src.explanation: Hydralazine is contraindicated in coronary artery disease, the elderly and ischemia, because vasodilation with reflex sympathetic activation raises cardiac workload.

items.html: Clonidine withdrawal. Abrupt withdrawal causes rebound hypertension, a class side effect that may be severe, so the drug must not be stopped suddenly.

src.question: A patient on clonidine runs out of tablets over a long weekend. What is the main danger?
src.explanation: Abrupt withdrawal hypertension is a class side effect, and clonidine withdrawal reactions may be severe, so the drug must not be stopped suddenly.

items.html: Hydralazine mechanism. It is not fully understood; proposed actions include increased cyclic GMP (via nitric oxide), renal prostaglandins and interference with calcium movement.

src.question: Which statement about hydralazine's mechanism of action is accurate?
src.explanation: The mechanism is not clear; proposed actions include increased cyclic GMP (via nitric oxide), renal prostaglandins and interference with calcium movement.

items.html: Non-selective beta blocker start. Cardiac output falls, so total peripheral resistance rises by reflex at first; mean arterial pressure falls only with chronic therapy as the baroreflex adjusts.

src.question: When a non-selective beta blocker is first started, what happens to total peripheral resistance?
src.explanation: Cardiac output falls, so peripheral resistance rises reflexly at first; mean arterial pressure falls only with chronic therapy as the baroreflex adjusts.

items.html: Labetalol. This third-generation agent has alpha-1 blockade in addition to beta blockade, and also has beta-2 agonist activity, giving direct vasodilation.

src.question: Besides beta blockade, what additional action does labetalol have?
src.explanation: Labetalol is a third-generation agent that blocks alpha-1 receptors and has beta-2 agonist activity, giving direct vasodilation.

items.html: Beta blockers and angiotensin II. Blocking renal beta-1 receptors on the juxtaglomerular cells, which mediate renin release, reduces renin and therefore angiotensin II.

src.question: How do beta blockers lower angiotensin II?
src.explanation: Beta-1 receptors on the juxtaglomerular cells mediate renin release, so blocking them reduces renin and therefore angiotensin II.

items.html: Beta blockers in COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease). They are contraindicated with bronchospasm because they block airway beta-2 receptors, reducing bronchial smooth muscle relaxation; about a third of patients with COPD develop bronchospasm.

src.question: Why are beta blockers contraindicated in a patient with COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) who has bronchospasm?
src.explanation: Blocking pulmonary beta-2 receptors reduces bronchial smooth muscle relaxation; about a third of COPD patients develop bronchospasm.

items.html: Beta blockers in type 1 diabetes. Beta blockers inhibit glycogenolysis, so hypoglycemia lasts longer, and they mask its adrenergic warning symptoms.

src.question: A patient with type 1 diabetes is starting propranolol. What should he be told about hypoglycemia?
src.explanation: Beta blockers inhibit glycogenolysis, so hypoglycemia lasts longer, and they mask its adrenergic warning symptoms.

items.html: AV conduction and calcium channel blockers. Both classes reduce the slow inward calcium current, but only non-dihydropyridines also decrease the channel's rate of recovery, which slows atrioventricular conduction.

src.question: Why do non-dihydropyridines slow atrioventricular conduction while dihydropyridines do not?
src.explanation: Both reduce the slow inward calcium current, but only the non-dihydropyridines also decrease the channel's rate of recovery, which slows atrioventricular conduction.

items.html: Verapamil and digoxin. Non-dihydropyridines inhibit P-glycoprotein, raising digoxin, tacrolimus, cyclosporine and carbamazepine; digoxin also adds a pharmacodynamic interaction.

src.question: How does verapamil raise digoxin levels?
src.explanation: Non-dihydropyridines inhibit P-glycoprotein, raising digoxin, tacrolimus, cyclosporine and carbamazepine; digoxin also adds a pharmacodynamic interaction.

items.html: Non-dihydropyridine adverse effects. Raised liver function tests are listed among them, and liver disease is a relative contraindication to diltiazem and verapamil.

src.question: Which laboratory change is listed among the adverse effects of non-dihydropyridines?
src.explanation: Elevations in liver function tests are listed, and liver disease is a relative contraindication to diltiazem and verapamil.

items.html: ACE inhibitors in left ventricular dysfunction. Give to all patients unless contraindicated. They reduce remodeling, afterload and preload, delay progression of heart failure, and reduce myocardial infarction and hospitalization.

src.question: Which statement describes ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors in left ventricular dysfunction?
src.explanation: They reduce remodeling, afterload and preload, delay progression of heart failure, and reduce myocardial infarction and hospitalization.

items.html: ACE inhibitor dry cough. It is not related to dose or agent, so lowering the dose will not stop it. It is more frequent in women and may require removing the ACE inhibitor if bothersome.

src.question: A patient asks whether the dry cough from her ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor will stop if the dose is lowered. What is accurate?
src.key: It is not related to dose or agent
src.explanation: The cough is not dose- or agent-related, is more frequent in women, and may require removing the ACE inhibitor if it is bothersome.

items.html: Angiotensin receptor blockers in pregnancy. They share the fetal morbidity and mortality of ACE inhibitors and are not given in the second and third trimesters, so they are not an acceptable substitute then.

src.question: A patient in her third trimester cannot take an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor. Is an angiotensin receptor blocker an acceptable substitute?
src.key: No, it is also avoided then
src.explanation: Angiotensin receptor blockers share the fetal morbidity and mortality and are not given in the second and third trimesters.

items.html: ACE inhibitors and bradykinin. The enzyme that makes angiotensin II also inactivates bradykinin, so blocking it slows bradykinin breakdown and bradykinin accumulates, the root of both the dry cough and angioedema.

src.question: Besides lowering angiotensin II, what does blocking angiotensin-converting enzyme do to bradykinin?
src.explanation: The same enzyme that makes angiotensin II also inactivates bradykinin, so bradykinin accumulates -- the root of both the dry cough and angioedema.

items.html: ACE inhibitors in pregnancy. They cause fetal morbidity and mortality, including birth defects and fetal death, and are contraindicated in the second and third trimesters.

src.question: Which statement about ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors in pregnancy is accurate?
src.key: Contraindicated in the second and third trimesters
src.explanation: They cause fetal morbidity and mortality, including birth defects and fetal death, so they are contraindicated in the second and third trimesters.

items.html: Angiotensin receptor blocker mechanism. They lower blood pressure by blocking AT1 (angiotensin II type 1) receptors, binding with high affinity and dissociating slowly for sustained blockade: vasodilation, less aldosterone and less sodium reabsorption.

src.question: How do angiotensin receptor blockers lower blood pressure?
src.explanation: They bind the AT1 (angiotensin II type 1) receptor with high affinity and dissociate slowly, giving sustained blockade: vasodilation, less aldosterone and less sodium reabsorption.

items.section_title: 3.9 · Objectives 9–10 — The treatment algorithm, monitoring and patient education
items.html: Reassessing blood pressure control. Reassess about 4 weeks after starting or titrating an antihypertensive. One or two titration steps are appropriate before modifying or adding medication.

src.question: After an antihypertensive is started or titrated, when should blood pressure control be reassessed?
src.explanation: Control is reassessed about 4 weeks after starting or titrating, and one or two titration steps are appropriate before modifying or adding medication.

items.html: Fibrate interactions. Fibrates such as gemfibrozil increase the anticoagulant effect of warfarin. They also interact with statins, ezetimibe and bile acid sequestrants.

src.question: A patient on warfarin is started on gemfibrozil. Which interaction is expected?
src.explanation: Fibrates increase the anticoagulant effect of warfarin; they also interact with statins, ezetimibe and bile acid sequestrants.

items.html: Niacin flushing. Flushing is prostaglandin mediated and is minimized by premedication with aspirin, so patients should take aspirin beforehand.

src.question: A patient starting niacin asks how to reduce the flushing. What is recommended?
src.explanation: Flushing is prostaglandin mediated and is minimized by premedication with aspirin.

items.html: Fibrate indication. Triglycerides over 1000 mg/dL are the primary indication for a fibrate. Fibrates lower triglycerides by 20 to 50%, and niacin by a similar amount.

src.question: A patient's only lipid problem is a triglyceride level over 1000 mg/dL. Which class is most appropriate?
src.explanation: Triglycerides over 1000 mg/dL are the primary fibrate indication; fibrates lower triglycerides by 20 to 50% (niacin by a similar amount).

items.html: Bile acid sequestrants and triglycerides. Resins may increase VLDL (very low-density lipoprotein) production and raise triglycerides, so they are avoided when triglycerides are high. On the lipid comparison they show no change or a rise in triglycerides.

src.question: Why are bile acid sequestrants avoided when triglycerides are high?
src.explanation: Resins may increase VLDL (very low-density lipoprotein) production, raising triglycerides; on the lipid comparison, resins show no change or a rise in triglycerides.

items.html: Resin effect on bile acids. When resins deplete the bile acid pool, cholesterol 7-alpha hydroxylase activity increases and converts more cholesterol to bile acids. The liver also adds LDL receptors, increasing VLDL and LDL removal.

src.question: When resins deplete the bile acid pool, which hepatic enzyme increases to convert cholesterol into bile acids?
src.explanation: Increased 7-alpha hydroxylase activity converts more cholesterol to bile acids, and the liver adds LDL receptors, increasing VLDL and LDL removal.

items.html: Ezetimibe use. Ezetimibe is typically added to a statin for dual inhibition: the statin blocks synthesis and ezetimibe blocks absorption, giving additional LDL (low-density lipoprotein) lowering.

src.question: How is ezetimibe typically used?
src.explanation: It pairs with a statin for dual inhibition -- the statin blocks synthesis, ezetimibe blocks absorption -- for additional LDL (low-density lipoprotein) lowering.

items.html: Long-term resin risk. Resins such as cholestyramine cause malabsorption of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K and of folic acid.

src.question: A patient has taken cholestyramine for years. Which deficiency is she at risk of?
src.explanation: Resins cause malabsorption of vitamins A, D, E and K and of folic acid.

items.html: Statin muscle toxicity. Muscle toxicity requires discontinuing the statin. Myopathy occurs in 0.2 to 0.4% of patients, with rare rhabdomyolysis.

src.question: A patient on simvastatin develops muscle toxicity. What is required?
src.explanation: The presence of muscle toxicity requires discontinuing the statin; myopathy occurs in 0.2 to 0.4% with rare rhabdomyolysis.

items.section_title: 4.9 · Objectives 9–10 — Guidelines, monitoring and patient education
items.html: Four statin benefit groups. Clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, such as after a myocardial infarction, is the first. The others are LDL above 190 mg/dL, diabetes at ages 40 to 75 with LDL 70 to 189, and high estimated risk.

src.question: Which patient falls into one of the four major statin benefit groups?
src.explanation: Clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease is the first benefit group; the others are LDL above 190 mg/dL, diabetes at 40 to 75 with LDL 70 to 189, and high estimated risk.

items.section_title: 4.9 · Objectives 9–10 — Guidelines, monitoring and patient education
items.html: Statin group for diabetes. Patients with diabetes aged 40 to 75 with LDL (low-density lipoprotein) 70 to 189 mg/dL and no clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease meet a statin benefit group.

src.question: Which patient with diabetes and no clinical cardiovascular disease meets a statin benefit group?
src.explanation: The diabetes group is ages 40 to 75 with LDL (low-density lipoprotein) 70 to 189 mg/dL and no clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

items.section_title: 4.9 · Objectives 9–10 — Guidelines, monitoring and patient education
items.html: ACC/AHA versus ATP III. The ACC/AHA (American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association) guideline starts moderate- or high-intensity statin therapy for the four benefit groups and does not treat to a specific LDL (low-density lipoprotein) target, unlike ATP III (Adult Treatment Panel III).

src.question: How does the ACC/AHA (American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association) cholesterol guideline differ from ATP III (Adult Treatment Panel III)?
src.key: It does not treat to an LDL target
src.explanation: It starts moderate- or high-intensity statin therapy for the four benefit groups and does not titrate to a specific LDL (low-density lipoprotein) target.

items.section_title: 4.9 · Objectives 9–10 — Guidelines, monitoring and patient education
items.html: LDL above 190 mg/dL. Individuals with LDL (low-density lipoprotein) above 190 mg/dL form one of the four statin benefit groups on that finding alone, whatever their other risk factors.

src.question: A 42-year-old with no diabetes and no cardiovascular disease has an LDL (low-density lipoprotein) cholesterol of 212 mg/dL. Does he fall into a statin benefit group?
src.explanation: Individuals with LDL above 190 mg/dL form one of the four statin benefit groups, whatever their other risk factors.

items.section_title: 1.4 · Objectives 1–3 — Allergy and the red eye
items.html: Rebound hyperemia. Naphazoline, a topical vasoconstrictor eye drop, causes rebound hyperemia after discontinuation if used for too long. Nasal decongestant sprays share the risk.

src.question: Which class of eye drop causes REBOUND HYPEREMIA if used for too long?
src.explanation: Naphazoline is a topical vasoconstrictor, and prolonged use leads to rebound hyperemia after discontinuation; nasal decongestant sprays share the risk.

items.section_title: 1.4 · Objectives 1–3 — Allergy and the red eye
items.html: Vasoconstrictor eye drop duration. Use is for the short term, less than two weeks. Prolonged use leads to rebound hyperemia after the drops are stopped.

src.question: A patient asks how long they may use a vasoconstrictor eye drop. What is the limit?
src.explanation: Vasoconstrictor drops are for short-term use under two weeks; prolonged use leads to rebound hyperemia after they are stopped.

items.section_title: 1.4 · Objectives 1–3 — Allergy and the red eye
items.html: Over-the-counter ophthalmic antihistamine. Ketotifen is the over-the-counter agent among the ophthalmic antihistamines.

src.question: Which ophthalmic antihistamine is available over the counter?
src.explanation: The over-the-counter agent among the ophthalmic antihistamines.

items.section_title: 1.4 · Objectives 1–3 — Allergy and the red eye
items.html: Ophthalmic antihistamines. Agents such as olopatadine have an onset within minutes, are dosed once or twice daily, and are typically preferred over mast cell stabilizers for ocular allergy.

src.question: Which class works within MINUTES and is typically preferred for ocular allergy?
src.explanation: Antihistamines have an onset within minutes, are dosed once or twice daily, and are preferred over mast cell stabilizers.

items.html: Glucocorticoids in the late-phase allergic reaction. Glucocorticoids such as prednisolone suppress the late phase by inhibiting phospholipase A2, cutting off arachidonic acid derived mediators at source. They also inhibit fibrin and collagen deposition, reducing scar formation.

src.question: Which class suppresses the LATE phase allergic reaction by inhibiting phospholipase A2?
src.explanation: The glucocorticoids, cutting off arachidonic acid derived mediators at source. They also inhibit fibrin and collagen deposition, reducing scar formation.

items.html: Aminoglycoside mechanism. Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin bind the 30S subunit to interfere with protein synthesis. Their ocular risk is corneal ulceration and reactive keratoconjunctivitis after several days.

src.question: Which ophthalmic antibiotic class binds the 30S subunit to interfere with protein synthesis?
src.explanation: The aminoglycoside mechanism. Its ocular risk is corneal ulceration and reactive keratoconjunctivitis after several days.

items.html: Fluoroquinolone mechanism. Fluoroquinolones such as moxifloxacin inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, so supercoiled DNA cannot relax and the double strand breaks.

src.question: Which ophthalmic antibiotic class inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, breaking double-stranded DNA?
src.explanation: The fluoroquinolone mechanism: supercoiled DNA cannot relax, and the strand breaks.

items.html: Ophthalmic antibiotic for corneal ulcers. Fluoroquinolones such as moxifloxacin are preferred for corneal ulcers or suspected Pseudomonas aeruginosa, though they are expensive and resistance is emerging.

src.question: Which ophthalmic antibiotic class is PREFERRED for corneal ulcers or suspected Pseudomonas aeruginosa?
src.explanation: The fluoroquinolones are the reach for ulcers and for the gram-negative rod, though they are expensive and resistance is emerging.

items.html: Aminoglycoside-specific ocular risk. Aminoglycosides such as tobramycin carry a risk of corneal ulceration and reactive keratoconjunctivitis after several days of use.

src.question: Which ophthalmic antibiotic class carries a risk of corneal ulceration and reactive keratoconjunctivitis after several days of use?
src.explanation: The aminoglycoside-specific risk, and one of the few adverse effects worth attaching to a single class.

items.html: Fluoroquinolone taste. Fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin can cause an unpleasant taste after instillation, reflecting nasolacrimal drainage carrying drug to the throat.

src.question: Which ophthalmic antibiotic class is associated with an unpleasant taste after instillation?
src.explanation: A fluoroquinolone effect, and it reflects nasolacrimal drainage carrying drug to the throat.

items.section_title: 1.4 · Objectives 1–3 — Allergy and the red eye
items.html: Antihistamine onset. An ophthalmic antihistamine acts within minutes, with fast onset but slower time to full efficacy. Allow two weeks to judge the full effect.

src.question: A 27-year-old starting an ophthalmic antihistamine asks when she will know if it is working. What do you tell her?
src.explanation: Correct — fast onset, slower to reach full efficacy. But allow two weeks to judge the full effect.

items.section_title: 1.4 · Objectives 1–3 — Allergy and the red eye
items.html: Redness-relief drop duration. Use should be no more than two weeks. If there is no improvement within 72 hours, the patient should stop and be seen.

src.question: A 24-year-old woman asks how long she can keep using her redness-relief drops. What do you tell her?
src.explanation: and if there is no improvement within 72 hours she should stop and be seen.

items.html: Fluoroquinolone for contact lens wearers. A fluoroquinolone is chosen for purulent conjunctivitis in a contact lens wearer once keratitis is excluded, because lens wearers are at high risk for Pseudomonas. The same class is preferred for corneal ulcers.

src.question: A 19-year-old contact lens wearer has purulent conjunctivitis. Keratitis has been excluded. Which class do you reach for, and why?
src.explanation: and the same class is preferred for corneal ulcers for the same reason. Because lens wearers are at high risk for Pseudomonas.

items.section_title: 1.8 · Objectives 9–10 — Administration, monitoring and patient education
items.html: Lacrimal duct occlusion. After a drop, occluding the duct limits nasolacrimal drainage and the systemic absorption that follows it. An ointment is too viscous to drain away, so there is nothing to block.

src.question: A 40-year-old is shown how to use both a drop and an ointment. Why must she cover the lacrimal duct after the DROP but not the ointment?
src.key: The ointment is too viscous to drain away
src.explanation: With a drop, occluding the duct limits nasolacrimal drainage and the systemic absorption that follows it. So there is nothing to block.

items.html: Dorzolamide local effects. Bitter taste (about a quarter of patients) and stinging on instillation (about a third) are both common with this class. Warning patients in advance improves adherence.

src.question: A 71-year-old on dorzolamide complains of a persistent bitter taste and stinging on instillation. What do you tell him?
src.key: Both are common with this class
src.explanation: and they are common enough that warning in advance improves adherence. Bitter taste in about a quarter and stinging in about a third.

items.html: Systemic effects of timolol drops. Systemic beta blockade can occur from a drop, causing worsening heart failure, bradycardia, heart block and increased airway resistance.

src.question: A 70-year-old on timolol drops develops fatigue and a heart rate of 48. What has happened?
src.explanation: Worsening heart failure, bradycardia, heart block and increased airway resistance are all possible from a drop.

items.section_title: 1.4 · Objectives 1–3 — Allergy and the red eye
items.html: No improvement with vasoconstrictor drops. No improvement within 72 hours is the trigger to stop the drop and see a provider, because something more serious may be going on.

src.question: A 41-year-old man has used a vasoconstrictor drop for three days with no improvement in his red eye. What should he do?
src.key: Stop the drop and see a provider
src.explanation: No improvement within 72 hours is the stated trigger for review. Because something more serious may be going on.

items.section_title: 1.4 · Objectives 1–3 — Allergy and the red eye
items.html: Rebound hyperemia counseling. Beyond about two weeks of daily redness-relief drops, stopping leaves the eye redder than it started. This is rebound hyperemia.

src.question: A 30-year-old man has used an over-the-counter redness-relief drop every day for a month. His eyes are redder than when he started. What has happened?
src.explanation: Beyond about two weeks, stopping leaves the eye redder than it started. This is the counseling point most worth carrying out of this topic.

items.html: Cyclosporine drops for dry eye. Beyond tear substitutes, cyclosporine drops are indicated for chronic dry eye with inflammation. They inhibit interleukin 2 production, reduce lacrimal inflammatory markers and raise tear production. Ocular burning is the commonest complaint.

src.question: A 58-year-old with rheumatoid arthritis has chronic dry eye with inflammation. Beyond tear substitutes, which agent is indicated?
src.explanation: It inhibits interleukin 2 production, reduces lacrimal inflammatory markers and raises tear production. Ocular burning is the commonest complaint.

items.section_title: 1.4 · Objectives 1–3 — Allergy and the red eye
items.html: Seasonal itchy, watery eyes. An ophthalmic antihistamine works within minutes and is typically preferred over mast cell stabilizers. Allow two weeks to judge full efficacy.

src.question: A 28-year-old has itchy, watery eyes each spring and wants something that works today. Which class do you choose?
src.explanation: and they are typically preferred over mast cell stabilizers. Allow two weeks to judge full efficacy. Which works within minutes.

items.section_title: 1.8 · Objectives 9–10 — Administration, monitoring and patient education
items.html: Instilling an eye drop. The single most important step is washing the hands thoroughly with soap and water, before anything else; the dropper must then not touch anything, so it stays sterile.

src.question: A patient is being taught to instill an eye drop. What is named as the single most important step?
src.key: Washing the hands thoroughly with soap and water
src.explanation: It is marked as the most important step, and it comes before anything else. The dropper must then not touch anything, so it stays sterile.

items.html: Ocular nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs in glaucoma. The adverse effect that matters most is a rise in intraocular pressure, which could undo glaucoma control; lacrimation, keratitis and irritation are the nuisance effects.

src.question: Which adverse effect of ocular nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs matters most in a patient who also has glaucoma?
src.explanation: Lacrimation, keratitis and irritation are the nuisance effects; the pressure rise is the one that interacts with an existing diagnosis and could undo glaucoma control.

items.section_title: 1.8 · Objectives 9–10 — Administration, monitoring and patient education
items.html: Conjunctivitis in contact lens wearers. Stop wearing lenses and resume after 24 hours clear of inflammation, dealing with the lens itself; eye makeup should go too, since it is the other reservoir.

src.question: A contact lens wearer has conjunctivitis. What is the advice about resuming lens wear?
src.key: Stop, and resume after 24 hours clear of inflammation
src.explanation: All three parts matter — stop, wait for a clear 24 hours, and deal with the lens itself. Eye makeup should go too, since it is the other reservoir.

items.section_title: 1.4 · Objectives 1–3 — Allergy and the red eye
items.html: Ocular H1 agents. They are not true antagonists but inverse agonists, still competing with histamine, so the effect depends on relative concentrations.

src.question: Ocular H1 agents are described as not really antagonists. What are they?
src.key: Inverse agonists, still competing with histamine
src.explanation: A true antagonist would simply occupy the site; an inverse agonist drives the receptor into an inactive state. They remain competitive with histamine, so the effect still depends on relative concentrations.

items.html: Ocular nonsteroidals and glaucoma. A rise in intraocular pressure matters most in a patient watched for glaucoma, because the drug given for inflammation pushes the very pressure that glaucoma treatment exists to lower.

src.question: Which adverse effect of the ocular nonsteroidals matters most in a patient already being watched for glaucoma?
src.explanation: The drug given for inflammation pushes the very pressure the glaucoma treatment exists to lower, so the two work against each other.

items.section_title: 1.4 · Objectives 1–3 — Allergy and the red eye
items.html: Ocular antihistamine adverse effects. Along with irritation and headache, they cause increased ocular dryness, worth mentioning to a patient who already has dry eyes.

src.question: Which adverse effect of ocular antihistamines is worth mentioning to a patient who already has dry eyes?
src.explanation: Along with irritation and headache, antihistamines can worsen dryness — which matters when dry eye is the background problem, since the treatment can aggravate the complaint.

items.section_title: 1.4 · Objectives 1–3 — Allergy and the red eye
items.html: Mast cell stabilizers. They are most useful in predictable seasonal allergy when the patient is intolerant of alternatives; their weaknesses are 5 to 14 days to full effect and often four times daily dosing.

src.question: For which patient are mast cell stabilizers described as most useful?
src.key: Predictable seasonal allergy, intolerant of alternatives
src.explanation: Their weaknesses — 5 to 14 days to full effect and often four times daily dosing — are tolerable if the season is predictable and can be pre-empted, and if the alternatives are not an option.

items.html: Macrolide mechanism. Erythromycin ointment and azithromycin solution act by inhibition of protein synthesis at the 50S ribosomal subunit, blocking transpeptidation so RNA-dependent protein synthesis stops.

src.question: Erythromycin ointment and azithromycin solution share a mechanism. What is it?
src.key: Inhibition of protein synthesis at the 50S ribosomal subunit
src.explanation: The macrolides block transpeptidation at the 50S subunit, so RNA-dependent protein synthesis stops and the organism dies. Knowing the subunit is what separates them from the aminoglycosides.

items.section_title: 1.1 · Objective 4 — Getting a drug into the eye, and out again
items.html: Blocking the tear ducts. Silicone plugs or cautery increase absorption because it stops the drop draining away; nasolacrimal drainage removes drug from the eye and sends it systemically.

src.question: Absorption can be deliberately increased by blocking the tear ducts with silicone plugs or cautery. Why does that work?
src.key: It stops the drop draining away
src.explanation: Nasolacrimal drainage removes drug from the eye and sends it systemically. Blocking it leaves more drug in contact with the cornea for longer — the same goal as thickening the formulation.

items.html: Goal in infectious conjunctivitis. Treatment aims to eradicate the infection and prevent long-term complications.

src.question: What is the stated goal of treating infectious conjunctivitis?
src.key: Eradicate the infection and prevent long-term complications
src.explanation: Both halves matter — clearing the organism is not the whole aim, because the reason to treat promptly is what an untreated infection leaves behind.

items.html: Ibuprofen adverse effects. The main ones fall on the gastrointestinal tract and the kidney (ulceration and bleeding, falling clearance, fluid retention and edema), both from prostaglandin blockade.

src.question: Which organ systems carry ibuprofen's main adverse effects?
src.key: The gastrointestinal tract and the kidney
src.explanation: Ulceration and bleeding at one end, falling clearance and edema at the other -- and both come from the same prostaglandin blockade. Fluid retention and edema come with the renal effects.

items.html: Ibuprofen with an anticoagulant. Prothrombin time is prolonged, with a risk of serious gastrointestinal bleeding; the combination is worse than either alone.

src.question: What happens when ibuprofen is combined with an anticoagulant?
src.explanation: Ibuprofen damages the mucosa and the anticoagulant stops the bleeding from being controlled, which is why the combination is worse than either alone. With a risk of serious gastrointestinal bleeding.

items.html: Acetaminophen and regular alcohol. The combination risks liver damage over time; neither is dangerous on its own at ordinary use.

src.question: What should a patient who drinks alcohol regularly be told about acetaminophen?
src.key: The combination risks liver damage over time
src.explanation: Neither is dangerous on its own at ordinary use, which is what makes the combination easy to arrive at without noticing.

items.html: Ibuprofen versus aspirin. At cyclooxygenase, ibuprofen inhibits reversibly rather than irreversibly, so the effect lifts as the drug clears and it is not used as an antiplatelet the way aspirin is.

src.question: How does ibuprofen differ from aspirin at cyclooxygenase?
src.key: It inhibits reversibly rather than irreversibly
src.explanation: The effect lifts as the drug clears, which is why ibuprofen is not used as an antiplatelet the way aspirin is.

items.html: Ketoconazole interactions. It inhibits CYP3A4, raising the level of anything cleared by that route, which is why it interacts with so many other medicines.

src.question: Why does ketoconazole interact with so many other medicines?
src.explanation: It raises the level of anything cleared by that route, which makes the interaction list a property of the enzyme rather than of any one drug pairing.

items.html: Otic anti-infectives. Available agents are ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin, and two steroid combinations: ciprofloxacin with dexamethasone, and neomycin with polymyxin B and hydrocortisone.

src.question: Which agents are listed as available otic anti-infectives?
src.key: Ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin, and two steroid combinations
src.explanation: Two plain fluoroquinolones and two combinations, and the combinations are where the restrictions live. In full: ciprofloxacin, ciprofloxacin with dexamethasone, neomycin with polymyxin B and hydrocortisone, and ofloxacin.

items.section_title: 2.1 · Objectives 1–3 — Antibiotics for ear, sinus and throat infections
items.html: Acute otitis media after recent antibiotics. In a child who finished antibiotics recently, amoxicillin-clavulanate is used instead, because recent exposure selects for beta-lactamase producers, which the clavulanate covers.

src.question: A child with acute otitis media finished a course of antibiotics three weeks ago. How does that change the choice?
src.explanation: Recent antibiotic exposure selects for beta-lactamase producers, and that is exactly what the clavulanate is there to cover.

items.section_title: 2.1 · Objectives 1–3 — Antibiotics for ear, sinus and throat infections
items.html: Acute otitis media without recent antibiotics. Amoxicillin, at a high dose, is the mainstay and first line; the high dose is what overcomes the resistant pneumococcus.

src.question: A child has acute otitis media and has had no antibiotics in the last month. What is the mainstay of therapy?
src.explanation: High-dose amoxicillin is first line, and the dose is high for a reason rather than by habit: it is what overcomes the resistant pneumococcus.

items.section_title: 2.1 · Objectives 1–3 — Antibiotics for ear, sinus and throat infections
items.html: Viral acute otitis media. Most cases are viral, or viral with bacteria alongside, which is one reason antibiotics are not automatic in every case.

src.question: Most acute otitis media involves a virus. What does that fact change?
src.key: It is one reason antibiotics are not automatic in every case
src.explanation: A majority of cases are viral, or viral with bacteria alongside, which is the argument against reaching for an antibiotic reflexively.

items.section_title: 2.1 · Objectives 1–3 — Antibiotics for ear, sinus and throat infections
items.html: Macrolides in acute otitis media. They remain an option for the penicillin-allergic patient but are a weak choice, because up to half of pneumococci are resistant to macrolides.

src.question: Why is a macrolide a weak choice in acute otitis media even when it is permitted?
src.key: Up to half of pneumococci are resistant to macrolides
src.explanation: It remains an option for the penicillin-allergic patient, but the resistance rate is the reason it is not a comfortable one.

items.section_title: 2.1 · Objectives 1–3 — Antibiotics for ear, sinus and throat infections
items.html: Viral versus bacterial rhinosinusitis. Symptoms beyond ten days, or worsening after five to six days, decide that an antibiotic is given; the timeline does the work because nothing on examination reliably separates the two.

src.question: What separates viral from bacterial rhinosinusitis, and so decides whether an antibiotic is given?
src.explanation: The timeline does the work, because nothing on examination reliably separates the two. Or worsening after five to six days.

items.html: Nasal corticosteroid side effects. They cause nosebleed, perforation and an unpleasant taste; all three are local, unlike a systemic steroid.

src.question: What are the described side effects of nasal corticosteroids?
src.key: Nosebleed, perforation and an unpleasant taste
src.explanation: All three are local, which is the trade-off that makes a nasal steroid different from a systemic one.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Objectives 1–6 — Histamine and the H1 antagonists
items.html: The flare. The redness spreading around the original insult comes from a reflex through axons causing vasodilation, a nerve reflex rather than direct spread of histamine.

src.question: What produces the flare, the redness spreading out around the original insult?
src.key: A reflex through axons causing vasodilation
src.explanation: It is a nerve reflex rather than direct spread of histamine, which is why the flare extends beyond where the histamine actually is.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Objectives 1–6 — Histamine and the H1 antagonists
items.html: H1 receptor effects on airways. H1 receptors raise smooth muscle tone and cause bronchoconstriction, so histamine itself is a bronchoconstrictor and H1 antagonists relax airway and gut smooth muscle.

src.question: What effect do H1 receptors have on smooth muscle and airways?
src.key: They raise smooth muscle tone and cause bronchoconstriction
src.explanation: This is why an H1 antagonist relaxes airway and gut smooth muscle, and why histamine itself is a bronchoconstrictor.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Objectives 1–6 — Histamine and the H1 antagonists
items.html: H2 receptor effect. Increased gastric acid secretion belongs to H2 rather than H1 receptors, which is why H2 blockers are stomach drugs while H1 blockers are allergy drugs.

src.question: Which effect belongs to H2 rather than H1 receptors?
src.explanation: It is the reason H2 blockers are stomach drugs while H1 blockers are allergy drugs.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Objectives 1–6 — Histamine and the H1 antagonists
items.html: Topical antihistamine adverse effects. Topical use is specifically associated with dermatitis and photosensitivity of the skin.

src.question: Which adverse effects are specifically associated with topical use of antihistamines?
src.key: Dermatitis and photosensitivity of the skin
src.explanation: Applying an antihistamine to skin can produce the kind of reaction it was meant to treat.

items.section_title: 2.9 · Objectives 1–7 — Cough: antitussives, expectorants and mucolytics
items.html: Goals of cough treatment. The aim is fewer, milder episodes and no complications; abolishing the cough is not the goal, since a productive cough is doing a job.

src.question: What are the stated goals of treating a cough?
src.key: Fewer, milder episodes and no complications
src.explanation: Note that abolishing the cough is not the goal, which matters because a productive cough is doing a job.

items.html: Topical nasal decongestant. Patients are told not to use it beyond a few days; exceeding that produces rebound congestion.

src.question: What is the central instruction for a patient given a topical nasal decongestant?
src.key: Do not use it beyond a few days
src.explanation: It is the whole safety message for this drug, and exceeding it is what produces rebound congestion.

items.html: Glaucoma pressure target. The general goal is a 20 to 30 percent reduction in intraocular pressure, expressed as a proportion rather than an absolute number, to prevent progressive optic nerve damage with the fewest side effects.

src.question: What is the general target for pressure reduction in glaucoma therapy?
src.key: A 20 to 30 percent reduction in intraocular pressure
src.explanation: The goal is expressed as a proportion rather than an absolute number, which matches the stated aim: prevent progressive optic nerve damage with the least risk and fewest side effects.

items.html: Mydriatic anticholinergics. Atropine, cyclopentolate and tropicamide produce mydriasis because they competitively block muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, the opposite of pilocarpine's action.

src.question: How do atropine, cyclopentolate and tropicamide produce mydriasis?
src.key: They competitively block muscarinic acetylcholine receptors
src.explanation: Blocking muscarinic receptors is the exact opposite of pilocarpine's action, which is why one dilates and the other constricts. They are used diagnostically and in uveitis to prevent synechiae and relieve ciliary spasm.

items.html: Combination therapy in glaucoma. More than one agent is often needed for targeting production and outflow together; combinations are synergistic and also cut the number of drops, which helps compliance.

src.question: Why is more than one agent often needed to control intraocular pressure?
src.explanation: Combinations are described as synergistic for exactly that reason, and they also cut the number of drops a patient has to manage, which helps compliance.

items.html: Ophthalmic alpha-2 agonists. They are contraindicated in children under two, from apnea risk.

src.question: In which patients are ophthalmic alpha-2 agonists contraindicated, and why?
src.key: Children under two, from apnea risk
src.explanation: A hard age contraindication, and the mechanism is the same central alpha-2 effect that makes imidazoline ingestion dangerous in toddlers. Worth holding alongside that question.

items.html: Pilocarpine in glaucoma. It lowers intraocular pressure because it activates muscarinic receptors on the ciliary muscle; contracting the muscle pulls on the trabecular meshwork and opens the drainage route.

src.question: How does pilocarpine lower intraocular pressure?
src.key: It activates muscarinic receptors on the ciliary muscle
src.explanation: Contracting the ciliary muscle pulls on the trabecular meshwork and opens the drainage route — an outflow drug achieved by a muscle action.

items.html: Clonidine. It lowers blood pressure by stimulating central alpha-2 receptors; as an alpha-2 and imidazoline agonist, it inhibits sympathetic outflow and increases parasympathetic activity.

src.question: How does clonidine lower blood pressure?
src.explanation: Clonidine is an alpha-2 and imidazoline agonist; stimulating central alpha-2A receptors inhibits sympathetic outflow and increases parasympathetic activity.

items.html: Direct vasodilators used alone. They lose effect over time because reflex responses cause tachyphylaxis: arteriolar dilation triggers reflex sympathetic activation (tachycardia, higher cardiac output, fluid retention, raised renin).

src.question: Why do direct vasodilators lose their effect over time when used alone?
src.explanation: Arteriolar dilation triggers reflex sympathetic activation (tachycardia, higher cardiac output, fluid retention, raised renin), producing tachyphylaxis.

items.html: Beta blockers in heart failure. Start at a very low dose and increase slowly, because beta blockers initially worsen heart failure symptoms.

src.question: How should a beta blocker be started in a patient with heart failure?
src.explanation: Beta blockers initially worsen heart failure symptoms, so they are started at a very low dose and increased slowly.

items.html: Calcium channel blockers and load. At therapeutic doses they lower afterload with no change in preload, because they do not reduce venous tone.

src.question: At therapeutic doses, how do calcium channel blockers affect preload and afterload?
src.key: Lower afterload, no change in preload
src.explanation: At therapeutic doses they do not reduce venous tone, so they decrease afterload without affecting preload.

items.html: Angiotensin II despite ACE inhibition. Angiotensin II can still be produced by other enzymes such as chymase (also trypsin and cathepsin), a limit of ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors that angiotensin receptor blockers get around.

src.question: Why can angiotensin II still be produced in a patient taking an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor?
src.explanation: Trypsin, cathepsin and chymase provide alternative routes to angiotensin II -- the limiting factor of ACE inhibitors that angiotensin receptor blockers get around.

items.html: ACE inhibitors in renal disease. Start with a low dose, increased slowly, because glomerular filtration can fall dramatically where renal blood flow depends on angiotensin II.

src.question: How should an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor be started in a patient with renal disease?
src.explanation: Because glomerular filtration can fall dramatically where renal blood flow depends on angiotensin II, the drug is used cautiously: low doses moved upward slowly.

items.html: Niacin and gout. Symptomatic gout is a relative contraindication because niacin raises uric acid; at larger doses it also raises liver enzymes and glucose.

src.question: Why is niacin a relative contraindication in a patient with symptomatic gout?
src.explanation: At larger doses niacin raises liver enzymes, glucose and uric acid, so gout and significant hyperuricemia are relative contraindications.

items.html: Statin with a fibrate. Combine them only with caution because of a higher risk of myopathy, as both classes can cause it; gemfibrozil is a relative contraindication with statins.

src.question: Why is a statin combined with a fibrate only with caution?
src.explanation: Both classes can cause myopathy, so they are combined cautiously; gemfibrozil is a relative contraindication with statins.

items.html: Niacin and glucose. Larger doses raise glucose and decrease glucose tolerance, making diabetes a relative contraindication.

src.question: What does niacin do to glucose control at larger doses?
src.explanation: Larger doses raise glucose and decrease glucose tolerance, making diabetes a relative contraindication.

items.html: Cholestyramine powder. Mix it in water or fruit juice; a pulpy drink masks the taste.

src.question: How should a patient prepare cholestyramine powder?
src.key: Mix it in water or fruit juice
src.explanation: Powders must be mixed with water or fruit juice, and a pulpy drink masks the taste.

items.section_title: 4.1 · Objectives 1–2 — Lipid transport, and the memory aid
items.html: LDL receptor activity. When it falls, LDL accumulates in plasma, driving atherosclerosis; most LDL-lowering classes work by raising receptor activity.

src.question: What happens when LDL (low-density lipoprotein) receptor activity falls?
src.explanation: Reduced receptor activity lets LDL particles build up in plasma, which leads to atherosclerosis; most LDL-lowering classes work by raising receptor activity.

items.html: Reducing statin myopathy risk. Use the lowest effective dose; also use caution in renal impairment and with fibrates, avoid other drug interactions, and monitor symptoms and laboratory values.

src.question: Which measure reduces the risk of statin myopathy?
src.explanation: Risk is also reduced by caution in renal impairment, caution with fibrates, avoiding other drug interactions, and monitoring symptoms and laboratory values.

items.html: Adenoviral conjunctivitis. There is no antiviral for it; it runs a self-limited course and is treated with symptomatic relief of irritation.

src.question: Adenoviral conjunctivitis is diagnosed. Which antiviral is indicated?
src.key: None — there is no antiviral for adenoviral conjunctivitis
src.explanation: It runs a self-limited course and is treated with symptomatic relief of irritation.

items.html: Adding a second glaucoma agent. Choose a different mechanism, for synergy and fewer drops: targeting multiple routes lowers pressure synergistically, and fewer drops improves compliance. Adding a drug of the same category is the wrong move.

src.question: A patient's pressure is not controlled on one agent. What is the principle behind adding a second?
src.key: Choose a DIFFERENT mechanism, for synergy and fewer drops
src.explanation: Targeting multiple routes lowers pressure synergistically, and fewer drops improves compliance. Adding a drug of the same category would be the wrong move.

items.html: Glaucoma therapy goal. The general goal is a 20 to 30 percent reduction in pressure, and therapy can be started in one eye to judge efficacy and tolerability.

src.question: What is the general goal of glaucoma therapy, in terms of pressure?
src.explanation: And therapy can be started in one eye to judge efficacy and tolerability.

items.html: Routes of lowering intraocular pressure. Brimonidine, an alpha adrenergic agonist, both increases outflow and decreases production; prostaglandins and cholinergics increase outflow, while beta blockers and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors decrease production.

src.question: Which two routes lower intraocular pressure, and which class does BOTH?
src.key: Brimonidine — it increases outflow AND decreases production
src.explanation: Alpha adrenergic agonists appear on both lists. Prostaglandins and cholinergics increase outflow; beta blockers and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors decrease production.

items.html: Prostaglandin analog cosmetic effects. Warn about longer lashes and iris color change, which matter more when only one eye is treated; conjunctival hyperemia is common too.

src.question: A 49-year-old woman starting a prostaglandin analog in one eye should be warned about which cosmetic effects?
src.key: Longer lashes and iris color change
src.explanation: and they matter more when only one eye is treated. Conjunctival hyperemia is common too.

items.html: Fungal corneal infiltrate risk. Long-term topical steroid use most raises the risk; immunosuppression, including topical steroids, sits alongside trauma, chronic surface disease and contact lens wear.

src.question: A 63-year-old is being assessed for a corneal infiltrate. Which of her features most raises the risk that it is FUNGAL?
src.explanation: Immunosuppression — including topical steroids — sits alongside trauma, chronic surface disease and contact lens wear.

items.html: Topical ocular antibiotics. They give very high local concentrations at the eye that an intravenous drug cannot, but more involved infection still needs systemic therapy.

src.question: A 36-year-old has a small peripheral corneal infection. Why can a topical antibiotic reach concentrations at the eye that an intravenous one cannot?
src.key: It gives very high LOCAL concentrations
src.explanation: Correct — and the trade-off is that more involved infection still needs systemic therapy.

items.section_title: 1.8 · Objectives 9–10 — Administration, monitoring and patient education
items.html: Resuming lenses after conjunctivitis. Lenses may resume when the eye is not inflamed and there has been no discharge for 24 hours; the lens should be discarded or disinfected, and eye makeup discarded too.

src.question: A 21-year-old contact lens wearer is treated for conjunctivitis. When may she resume her lenses?
src.key: When the eye is not inflamed and there has been no discharge for 24 hours
src.explanation: and she should get rid of her eye makeup too. With the lens discarded or disinfected.

items.html: Raised pressure in glaucoma. Treat those with risk factors; monitor those without. Raised pressure alone is not automatically a prescription, and in the absence of risk factors you watch for the change that would make it a disease.

src.question: Which patients with raised pressure are treated, and which are monitored?
src.key: Treat those with risk factors; monitor those without
src.explanation: Raised pressure alone is not automatically a prescription. Risk factors decide, and in their absence you watch for the change that would make it a disease.

items.html: Verapamil and simvastatin. Verapamil raises simvastatin levels through CYP3A4 inhibition. Non-dihydropyridines inhibit CYP3A4, raising atorvastatin, lovastatin and simvastatin, as well as carbamazepine, propranolol, tacrolimus and cyclosporine.

src.question: A patient on simvastatin is started on verapamil and develops muscle aches. By what mechanism does verapamil raise simvastatin levels?
src.explanation: Non-dihydropyridines inhibit CYP3A4, raising atorvastatin, lovastatin and simvastatin, as well as carbamazepine, propranolol, tacrolimus and cyclosporine.

items.html: Aspirin contraindications. Bleeding disorders, pregnancy, and children with fever from viral illness; the three involve unrelated mechanisms (bleeding risk, pregnancy, and Reye's), so the list has to be remembered rather than derived.

src.question: Which situations are listed as contraindications to aspirin?
src.explanation: Three unrelated mechanisms -- bleeding risk, pregnancy, and Reye's -- which is why the list has to be remembered rather than derived. Children with fever from viral illness.

items.html: Aspirin versus acetaminophen for fever in a child. Aspirin in a child with viral illness such as influenza risks Reye's syndrome, which is why acetaminophen became the default antipyretic in children.

src.question: A child has fever during influenza. Why is acetaminophen preferred over aspirin?
src.key: Aspirin in a child with viral illness risks Reye's syndrome
src.explanation: This is the everyday consequence of the Reye's association, and it is why acetaminophen became the default antipyretic in children.

items.html: Diuretic plus dexamethasone. Monitor potassium, since both drugs lower it; two drugs pushing the same electrolyte the same way can bring a patient to a dangerous level without either drug being at fault alone.

src.question: A patient on a diuretic is started on dexamethasone. What should be monitored?
src.key: Potassium, since both drugs lower it
src.explanation: Two drugs pushing the same electrolyte the same way, which is how a patient arrives at a dangerous level without either drug being at fault alone.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Objectives 1–6 — Histamine and the H1 antagonists
items.html: Antihistamine drying of secretions. Antihistamines reduce nasal and bronchial secretions during an allergic reaction through their antimuscarinic action; the drying is a muscarinic effect rather than a histamine one, so second generation agents dry you out less.

src.question: How do antihistamines reduce nasal and bronchial secretions during an allergic reaction?
src.explanation: The drying is a muscarinic effect rather than a histamine one, which is why the second generation agents dry you out less.

items.html: Topical ophthalmic beta blocker. It can produce systemic bradycardia, heart block and bronchoconstriction, because nasolacrimal absorption avoids first-pass metabolism, so a topical beta blocker can do everything a systemic one does.

src.question: Which systemic adverse effects can a topical ophthalmic beta blocker produce?
src.explanation: A drop is not a local-only treatment — nasolacrimal absorption avoids first-pass metabolism, so a topical beta blocker can do everything a systemic one does.

items.html: Beta blockade in exertional angina. It prolongs time to symptoms: blunting the rise in heart rate and contractility lengthens the time to the angina-provoking heart rate and prolongs exercise time.

src.question: How does beta blockade help a patient with exertional angina?
src.explanation: By blunting the rise in heart rate and contractility, beta blockade lengthens the time to the angina-provoking heart rate and prolongs exercise time.

items.html: Rising liver enzymes on atorvastatin. Lower the dose or pause it; liver enzyme rises occur in 0.5 to 2.5% of patients in a dose-dependent manner and are managed by reducing the dose or stopping until levels return to normal.

src.question: A patient's liver enzymes rise after starting atorvastatin. What is the recommended management?
src.key: Lower the dose or pause it
src.explanation: Liver enzyme rises occur in 0.5 to 2.5% of patients in a dose-dependent manner and are managed by reducing the dose or stopping until levels return to normal.

items.html: Nonselective beta blocker in the eye. It is more efficacious but worse tolerated because there are more beta 2 receptors in the eye; blocking both gives more effect, at the cost of beta 2 effects elsewhere.

src.question: Why is a NONSELECTIVE beta blocker more efficacious in the eye but worse tolerated?
src.key: There are more beta 2 receptors in the eye
src.explanation: So blocking both gives more effect, at the cost of beta 2 effects elsewhere.

items.html: First-line LDL lowering. Atorvastatin is first line when LDL (low-density lipoprotein) lowering drugs are indicated; statins are the most efficacious and best tolerated agents.

src.question: Which drug is FIRST LINE when LDL (low-density lipoprotein) lowering drugs are indicated?
src.explanation: Statins are the most efficacious and best tolerated agents and are first line for LDL lowering.

items.html: Latanoprost twice daily. Using latanoprost twice daily does not lower pressure further; it inhibits the effect, which is counterintuitive.

src.question: A 66-year-old on latanoprost asks whether using it twice daily would lower his pressure further. What do you tell him?
src.explanation: and counterintuitive enough to be worth stating plainly.

items.html: Azithromycin versus erythromycin eye preparations. Azithromycin solution is dosed twice daily, against four or more times a day for erythromycin ointment, which helps compliance, but azithromycin is considerably more expensive, so erythromycin remains the common choice.

src.question: Azithromycin solution is dosed twice daily while erythromycin ointment may be needed four or more times a day. Why is azithromycin still not the usual choice?
src.explanation: The dosing advantage is real and helps compliance, but cost keeps it from being used as often clinically. Erythromycin remains the common one.

items.html: Systemic corticosteroid contraindication. Systemic fungal infection is a specific contraindication, because a drug that suppresses immunity makes a disseminated fungal infection worse.

src.question: Which infection is specifically a contraindication to systemic corticosteroids?
src.explanation: A drug that suppresses immunity given to someone with a disseminated fungal infection makes the infection worse.

items.section_title: 2.10 · Objectives 9–10 — Protocols, monitoring and patient education
items.html: Nasal spray hand technique. Use the right hand for the left nostril and the left hand for the right: crossing hands angles the spray away from the septum, which is where nosebleed and perforation happen.

src.question: Why is a patient told to use the right hand for the left nostril and the left hand for the right?
src.key: It angles the spray away from the septum
src.explanation: Crossing hands sets the angle automatically, and the septum is what nosebleed and perforation happen to.

items.html: Topical beta blocker in a patient with asthma. Betaxolol is safer because it is beta-1 selective; beta-2 receptors mediate bronchodilation, so blocking them raises airway resistance. Carteolol, timolol and levobunolol are non-selective.

src.question: A patient with asthma needs a topical beta blocker for glaucoma. Which agent is safer, and why?
src.key: Betaxolol, because it is beta-1 selective
